notes.omuliro: Also “hot”: maji ya moto (hot water). Motoni: on the fire.
notes.kitunguu: Plural: vitunguu. Kitunguu saumu is garlic.

guidebook.intro: Swahili coast cooking mixes African, Arab and Indian kitchens. Follow a recipe for pilau, and learn the words a cook shouts across the kitchen.

tips.title: -ni: in, on, at
body: Add **-ni** to a noun to mean “in”, “on” or “at” it: **moto** (fire) → **motoni** (on the fire), **soko** → **sokoni** (at the market), **shule** → **shuleni** (at school).
You’ve been using it since **jikoni** (in the kitchen) and **nyumbani** (at home).

tips.title: Recipe verbs
body: Recipes are a string of commands: **Kata**, **kaanga**, **ongeza**, **changanya**. To two or more cooks, add **-ni**: **Kateni vitunguu!**
**-sha** often means “make it do”: **chemka** (boil, by itself) gives **chemsha** (bring to the boil), **safi** (clean) gives **safisha** (make clean).

culture.title: Rice has three names
body: Rice growing in the field is **mpunga**, uncooked grains are **mchele**, and cooked rice is **wali**. Spiced with meat it becomes **pilau**, the dish for weddings and Eid.

culture.title: Come and eat
body: If you arrive while people are eating, you will hear **Karibu chakula!** It’s a real invitation. Saying **Asante, nimeshiba** (thanks, I’m full) is a polite way to decline.
